beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: nothing new, a title

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: A slogan. I can't tell yet what compounds, or for whom.

beats.trigger: Revisit the crux, what would have to be true, pre-mortem.
beats.got: Homework that points back to earlier modules. I don't remember what 'crux' means exactly.

beats.trigger: **Produce** a strategy kernel, suggested agent set, and two-week plan from your files
beats.got: The outputs are strategy and a plan, so it's not only tool tricks. Still no word about people.

beats.trigger: The room-scale exercise uses a separate shared deliberation folder, so participant files stay out of your local stack.
beats.got: We work in a shared folder where everyone's agents read each other's files. Whose data goes in there, and who has approved it?

beats.trigger: You watch one agent build another on real input.
beats.got: The point of the session is to see an agent produce an agent.

beats.trigger: You describe an agent; the coding agent builds it.
beats.got: I describe it in words and the tool builds it. That's clearer than I expected.

beats.trigger: On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand.
beats.got: Four lines: the gap, the job, what it reads, what it writes. For me that's the weekly people-metrics summary I now assemble by hand.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: I paste the prompt and wait. I can't judge it from what's shown, but I'd run it.

beats.trigger: "You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."
beats.got: I can push back in plain language and make the agent show where each claim came from. That matters for anything I'd show an HR partner.

beats.trigger: Agents start privately enough to have a point of view, ask you for missing judgment when useful, then publish in the shared proposal folder.
beats.got: Twenty agents debate each other around a company problem. It's a lot of moving parts and it's hard to picture.

beats.trigger: Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references.
beats.got: Someone has at least thought about sensitive data. But 'redact it yourself' is a thin safeguard for employee data. I would want the DPO and the works council involved.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: Each agent forms its own view before seeing the others, so the room doesn't just converge on the loudest voice. That's sensible.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: Agents read their neighbours' stances and look for blind spots.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: There is a visible trail of who changed their mind. I like that. It also looks a bit like surveillance, depending on who reads it.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: A central agent chooses the best ideas and doesn't just take the middle. I'm not sure who the synthesizer answers to.

beats.trigger: Your agents read that instruction file in the next step, so you do not prompt the cross-pollination yourself.
beats.got: The central agent steers everyone's agents midway through. 'Instruction injection' is jargon I don't like hearing, and it was not explained.

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: The first choice is only a draft and gets challenged.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: The sponsor decides which assumptions to test, not the agents. That is the answer I can take to my leadership team about who decides.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: We finish with three files: a kernel, an agent set and a plan.

beats.trigger: Likeliest unseen pre-mortem failure; one early warning sign.
beats.got: The kernel is a structured one-pager: diagnosis, policy, experiments, risks. I could use that format for a people question.

beats.trigger: "You are now agent builders. You have built agents that do real work on your company's data."
beats.got: A rehearsed identity line. I'm a bit allergic to it, and I'd say it differently in my own organisation.

beats.trigger: The forum didn't converge on the first try. Pushback rounds were the work.
beats.got: It's honest that the first answer wasn't good and the pushback did the work. That kind of understatement earns some trust from me.

beats.trigger: The room ran on its own for an hour: agents read each other's files, published, and something at the centre chose.
beats.got: The lecture reflects on the hour we just spent.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The skill that matters is specifying well, not building. That is a skill I can train in people, and it says something about roles.

beats.trigger: Access was instant and complete. What the room took up from each other is the smaller number.
beats.got: Having access to everything is not the same as using it. This is exactly my rollout problem: we can give everyone the tool, but the number that matters is who uses it.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources
beats.got: Agents must cite which file each claim came from, or they make up what they never read.

beats.trigger: The plan names the wall your company hits first: data access, runtime platform, or discoverability.
beats.got: There are three obstacles. For me the first is data access, and employee data goes through the works council. The slide doesn't say that.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: The tools will change, but how you put the parts together will last.

beats.trigger: Nobody in this room knows yet, and the people running this training do not know either.
beats.got: The trainers admit they don't know what will be obsolete. Honest, and the opposite of hype. I trust it more.

beats.trigger: What your company knows about its own work gets better only when somebody writes it down and somebody else picks it up.
beats.got: The bottleneck is organisational learning, which is a people question. This is the first moment the day became about my job.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: I can ask my leadership team: what would make us drop this plan? Most won't have an answer.

beats.trigger: Hold that doubt as you did then.
beats.got: Nothing closed and nothing was checked. The doubt is left with me deliberately.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the session, rewrites the most load-bearing file in place
beats.got: An agent reviews the session and rewrites a key file. I can't tell from here how well it works.

beats.trigger: The agent audits itself, so the summary is not neutral.
beats.got: Don't trust the agent's own summary. Ask it for the critique that didn't change anything.

beats.trigger: Parts hold; the model rotates.
beats.got: Four bullet points. None of them are about people.

beats.trigger: The agent that matters in six months is one nobody in this room has thought of.
beats.got: The point is the ability to build the next agent, not the ones built today. I like the modesty, but the closing line is a bit pat.

take_homes: Access is not uptake. The number of folders the kernel actually cites is my rollout metric, and I should know it before I promise my board a percentage.
Organisational learning is the bottleneck, not the model: what the company knows only improves when someone writes it down and someone else picks it up. That is an HR question.
A question for my leadership team: what would have to show up for us to drop this plan? Agents must also cite their sources, and a human decides.

monday.move: Draft the extension brief for a weekly people-metrics summary agent, and write down which employee data it would touch. Then ask the DPO and the works council representative before running it on anything real.
monday.who: Me, then one HR business partner, then the DPO
monday.when: Draft Monday; the conversations with the DPO and the works council representative that same week
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO or the works council says the data can't go into the tool, I stop and use made-up sample data only.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet. The module's advice to redact salary references yourself is not enough.

misconception.why: The module never talks about roles or headcount, so my belief that agents replace headcount first was neither tested nor challenged. 'Specifying well is the harder half' hints that the work changes rather than disappears, but I still don't know which roles.

one_line: It was a good hands-on day, and the line about access not being uptake is worth the price. But it never said what this means for the people, and I'd have to take that question to the DPO myself.
